results.title: AWS stealthily raises GPU prices by 15 percent
highlights:
AWS has reportedly raised prices for some GPU-backed cloud instances by about 15%, adding fresh pressure to teams already struggling with the cost of AI infrastructure. The change matters because GPUs are the core fuel for training, fine-tuning, and serving modern machine learning models, and even modest percentage increases can translate into substantial monthly spend for high-usage customers.

...

AWS has reportedly raised prices by about 15% on a range of GPU-backed cloud instances, changing the economics for customers that rent accelerated compute by the hour rather than buying hardware outright. The increase appears to affect on-demand GPU instance pricing, the most visible and flexible purchasing model for teams that spin up capacity for training runs, inference endpoints, rendering jobs, simulations, or experimentation. For customers used to treating AWS GPU capacity as an elastic utility, the change means the same workload can now produce a materially higher monthly bill without any change in model size, traffic, or engineering behavior.

The affected services are centered on Amazon EC2 GPU instance families, including instance types commonly used for machine learning and high-performance computing. These include accelerator-heavy families such as P-series instances for training and large-scale compute, G-series instances for inference, graphics, and lighter ML workloads, and newer high-end configurations built around Nvidia data center GPUs. Customers using managed AWS services may also feel the increase indirectly when those services rely on EC2 GPU capacity underneath, especially where pricing is tied to provisioned accelerated instances or endpoint runtime.

### Where customers are most likely to notice the change

- EC2 on-demand GPU instances: Teams paying hourly or per-second rates for GPU virtual machines are likely to see the clearest increase.
- Machine learning training jobs: Long-running model training, fine-tuning, and distributed experiments become more expensive when GPU-hours rise in price.
- Inference workloads: Applications serving AI models on GPU instances may see higher steady-state costs, especially at high utilization or always-on capacity.
- Managed ML platforms: Services such as Amazon SageMaker can be affected when notebooks, training jobs, processing jobs, or hosted endpoints use impacted GPU instance types.
- Research and simulation workloads: HPC users running CUDA-based simulations, rendering pipelines, or scientific workloads on AWS GPUs may face higher project costs.

The practical change for customers is not only the higher list price but the reduced margin for inefficient usage. Idle GPU instances, oversized training clusters, underutilized inference endpoints, and exploratory books left running now waste more money than before. A 15% increase can also compound quickly because GPU spend is often concentrated in fewer, more expensive resources. For example, a team spending $100,000 per month on affected GPU capacity could see an additional $15,000 in monthly costs before accounting for growth in usage or data transfer, storage, and orchestration expenses.

The price move also matters because GPU capacity is often purchased through a mix of on-demand instances, reserved capacity, Savings Plans, capacity reservations, and spot instances. Customers with existing commitments may be insulated for some workloads until those agreements renew, while teams relying heavily on on-demand capacity can feel the change immediately. Spot pricing may not move in lockstep with list prices, but it is still influenced by supply and demand, and interruption risk can make spot unsuitable for some training and production inference use cases.

...

AWS’s reported 15% increase changes the comparison math for teams shopping for GPU capacity, but it does not make the market easy to rank. GPU pricing varies heavily by region, instance generation, commitment term, interconnect, storage, data transfer, and whether the workload needs reserved capacity or can tolerate interruptions. On-demand prices for high-end NVIDIA GPU instances are often only one line item; the real bill also includes EBS or local NVMe storage, networking, managed Kubernetes, monitoring, model artifacts, and data egress.

...

Specialized providers such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Crusoe, Paperspace, RunPod, and other GPU-focused platforms have become more relevant as large clouds raise prices or ration access. These providers can undercut hyperscaler on-demand rates for certain NVIDIA GPUs, especially when customers need raw compute rather than a full cloud platform. ... The trade-off is

...

AWS’s reported 15% increase is unlikely to be the last pricing move in cloud AI infrastructure. GPU supply remains tight, model training runs are getting larger, and inference traffic is moving from experiments into production systems that serve real users around the clock. The next phase of pricing will likely be less about a single hourly rate and more about how providers package scarce accelerators, networking, storage, support, and committed capacity into bundled offers.

results.title: Signwl GPU Price Index (SGPI) — Daily Series and Methodology
highlights: The Signwl GPU Price Index (SGPI) is a daily reference series for the cost of cloud GPU compute, published in two distinct forms: SGPI Level — an observation-weighted average price in USD per hour, blended across spot, on-demand, 1-year reserved, and 3-year reserved pricing tiers from the four major public cloud providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure). SGPI Index — a chain-linked, base-100 index (base = 100 on 2026-02-01), computed as a weighted geometric mean of daily price relatives across basket items present on both adjacent days. Designed to isolate pure price movement from changes in basket composition. This deposit is the version 1.0 snapshot. It contains the full daily time series, the complete methodology specification (with a worked example, entry/exit rules, revision policy, and change log), and a README with data dictionary and citation guidance. The live series is updated daily at 06:30 UTC and is available at https://signwl.com/indices/sgpi. The live methodology is maintained at https://signwl.com/indices/sgpi/methodology. This Zenodo deposit is the canonical, version-controlled snapshot for citation; new major-version deposits will follow when the methodology changes substantively. Published and maintained by Signwl — independent market intelligence for AI compute and infrastructure markets.

results.title: How Much Does PyTorch Cost on Cloud GPUs? 2026 Pricing Guide | Markaicode
highlights:
PyTorch itself is free; the real cost is H100 GPU compute, which runs $1.50–$11.00 per hour depending on cloud, region, and commitment as of August 2026.

...

> Quick Answer: PyTorch itself is free and open-source — you pay for the cloud GPUs underneath it. As of August 2026, on-demand NVIDIA H100 compute lists at roughly $6.88/GPU-hour on AWS P5 and roughly $10.98/GPU-hour on GCP A3, while spot or preemptible H100 capacity on either cloud can drop to $1.50–$3.00/GPU-hour. A hobby workload under 100 GPU-hours/month typically runs $400–$700; production inference with autoscaling runs $4,000–$10,000/month; enterprise training clusters above 5,000 GPU-hours/month typically run $30,000–$60,000/month before reserved discounts. The single biggest cost driver is idle GPU time between experiments, not the sticker price itself.

...

- On-demand GPU-hour rates vary by nearly 4x across AWS, GCP, and Azure for the identical NVIDIA H100 chip — but that spread mostly reflects networking (EFA vs equivalent), reserved-capacity discounts, and regional availability, not raw silicon.
- Chasing the cheapest listed per-GPU rate without checking real-world utilization is a common trap: a team paying $3/hour but sitting idle 60% of the time spends more than a team paying $7/hour at 90% utilization.
- Framework choice (PyTorch vs TensorFlow vs JAX) changes GPU-hours consumed per experiment by 15–20%, which usually matters more than which cloud you pick.
- Reserved and committed-use discounts only pay off above a specific utilization threshold — committing before you know your real usage pattern is the most common budget mistake in this category (see §14 break-even math).
- Before optimizing anything, confirm you're reading current list prices: cloud GPU pricing has changed materially even in the past 12 months (AWS cut P5/P4d on-demand rates by up to 45% in mid-2025), so screenshots or blog posts more than a few months old are unreliable.

...

PyTorch is billed indirectly through cloud GPU compute. The three things that actually drive your bill are: (1) which GPU generation and cloud you rent from, (2) how much of that capacity sits idle, and (3) whether you're on-demand, spot/preemptible, or reserved. At small scale (under 100 GPU-hours/month) expect low hundreds of dollars; at startup/production scale (1,000–2,000 GPU-hours/month) expect $5,000–$15,000; at enterprise training scale (5,000+ GPU-hours/month) expect $30,000–$70,000, with reserved commitments cutting that by roughly 40% if utilization stays high.

...

- AWS P5 specs (8× H100, 640GB HBM3, 3,200 Gbps EFA) and the June 2025 official price cut (up to 45% off on-demand P5/P4d rates) — [VERIFIED S0], confirmed directly against AWS's own product and announcement pages.
- AWS S3 internet egress: $0.09/GB after a 100GB/month free tier — [VERIFIED S0], confirmed verbatim in AWS's own S3 pricing page billing examples.
- AWS P5 on-demand rate ($6.88/GPU-hour, $55.04/hr for p5.48xlarge) and GCP A3 on-demand rate (~$10.98/GPU-hour, ~$87.83/hr for a3-highgpu-8g) — [EDITORIAL S2, as of Aug 2026]. Disclosed limitation: AWS's and GCP's own pricing pages render their rate tables via client-side JavaScript, which this SOP's verification tooling cannot extract; the AWS Price List Bulk API (a genuine S0 source) is also outside this tooling's reach. These per-hour figures are therefore cross-corroborated across three independent, recently-updated trackers (Thunder Compute, GMI Cloud) rather than read directly off the vendor page. They are directionally consistent with AWS's official 2025 price-cut percentage above, but you should re-confirm the exact rate on the AWS EC2 pricing page or AWS Pricing Calculator before committing a budget — this is the one category of number in this article that has not been verified against the vendor's own page.
- S3 Standard storage ($0.023/GB/month) — [VENDOR-STATED S1], a long-stable published rate not independently re-confirmed against the current page's rate table (same JS-rendering limitation as above).
- 1-year Reserved/Savings Plan discount (~40%) — [VENDOR-STATED S1], within the range AWS states publicly for P5 cost reductions; treat as illustrative rather than a quoted contract rate.

...

| Tier | Monthly GPU-Hours (H100) | Estimated Monthly Cost (AWS on-demand) | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hobby / Research | < 100 | $400–$700 | Single developer fine-tuning, experimentation |
| Startup / SaaS Inference | 100–1,000 | $700–$6,900 | Real-time inference with autoscaling, small models |
| Mid-Market Training | 1,000–5,000 | $6,900–$34,400 | Foundation model fine-tuning, batch inference |
| Enterprise / Pre-training | 5,000+ | $34,400–$70,000+ | Large-scale distributed training, 70B+ models |

As of August 2026, USD, AWS P5 on-demand rate of $6.88/GPU-hour. GCP A3 on-demand runs roughly 60% higher per GPU-hour.

...

- GPU compute — the dominant line item. AWS p5.48xlarge (8× H100) on-demand runs $55.04/hr ($6.88/GPU-hour); GCP a3-highgpu-8g runs roughly $87.83/hr (~$10.98/GPU-hour). A 7B-parameter model trained for one epoch on 1B tokens on 8 H100s consumes roughly 80–120 GPU-hours depending on sequence length and batch size.
- Storage — model weights and datasets. S3 Standard costs $0.023/GB/month; a 140GB checkpoint (70B model, fp16) costs about $3.22/month to store — negligible next to compute.
- Egress — data leaving the cloud region. AWS charges $0.09/GB after a 100GB/month free tier (confirmed directly on AWS's own S3 pricing page). Moving checkpoints between regions frequently is the main way this adds up; keeping training data and outputs in one region avoids it almost entirely.

...

Reserved (Savings Plan) pricing on AWS P5 trades a roughly 40% lower hourly rate for a 1-year commitment to pay for that capacity whether or not you use it. That means reserved pricing only wins above a specific utilization threshold — below it, you're paying for idle hours you'd never have been billed for on-demand.

Break-even utilization = (Reserved hourly rate × hours in commitment period) ÷ On-demand hourly rate

...

PyTorch itself is free; the cost comes entirely from the cloud GPU compute underneath it, which as of August 2026 runs roughly $6.88/GPU-hour on-demand for an H100 on AWS P5, or $1.50–$3.00/GPU-hour on spot/preemptible capacity.

results.title: IREN Stock Is Already Up 58% in 2026. Nvidia Could Keep Taking Shares Higher.
highlights:
Bitcoin mining already demands enormous amounts of electricity and large-scale data center infrastructure, the very same backbone required to power advanced AI chips and cloud computing workloads. Leveraging its existing crypto mining operations, IREN rapidly transformed its facilities into high-powered, server-packed AI data centers, positioning itself squarely in the middle of the generative AI boom. Excitement around the broader neocloud space accelerated further on May 21 after chip giant Nvidia (NVDA) CFO Colette Kress disclosed that rental pricing for Nvidia’s powerful H100 GPUs continues to rise. 

According to Kress, H100 rental prices are up roughly 20% year-to-date (YTD), while A100 cloud GPU pricing has climbed nearly 15%. The comments ignited fresh momentum across the neocloud sector, sending shares of companies, including IREN, up 10.2% in a single session. The rally came just weeks after IREN announced a major five-year AI infrastructure cloud services agreement with Nvidia, a deal that further amplified bullish sentiment surrounding the stock. 

Under the partnership, IREN will provide Nvidia with managed GPU cloud services for the chip giant’s internal AI and research workloads, including orchestration and cluster management software developed in collaboration with Mirantis. The contract will be supported by air-cooled Blackwell platform systems deployed across roughly 60MW of IREN’s existing data center capacity at its Childress, Texas campus. Altogether, the agreement carries an estimated value of approximately $3.4 billion over five years.
